prompt: Two workers sat almost idle, and the fifth copy of `big` still stayed `Pending`. Why?
hint: What does the scheduler add up?

choices.text: The nodes were busier than they looked
choices.why: The shop used almost no CPU; usage was not the problem.

choices.text: Only 800m was left unreserved on each
choices.why: Right. The scheduler compares requests with allocatable, and 1500m did not fit.

choices.text: Five copies exceed the Deployment's limit
choices.why: A Deployment has no such limit.

choices.text: The image was still being pulled
choices.why: The event said `Insufficient cpu`.

prompt: `kubectl describe node` showed `3200m (80%)` of CPU requested on `shop-worker`, which ran two copies of `big` at 1500m. Where did the other 200m come from?
hint: Not every pod on a node is yours.

choices.why: That is already subtracted from allocatable, not added to requests.

choices.text: Rounding up 1500m to the next CPU
choices.why: Requests are added exactly, in millicores.
A pending pod is on no node, so it reserves nothing.

choices.text: The network plugin's pod and a CoreDNS copy
choices.why: Right. Each requests 100m.

prompt: A container has a CPU limit of 200m and does work that takes 50 ms of CPU when unthrottled. Roughly how long does it take under the limit?
hint: 200m is a fifth of a CPU.

choices.why: That would be no throttling at all.
Right. It runs 20 ms in each 100 ms period, so 50 ms of work spans about 250.
CPU limits throttle; they never kill.
A limit can only slow a container down.

prompt: A pod restarts every few minutes, and its last state reads `OOMKilled`, exit code 137. What happened?

choices.text: It ran over its CPU limit
choices.why: A CPU limit throttles; it does not kill.
That ends with the kubelet restarting it, and the reason is not `OOMKilled`.
Right. The kernel killed it; 137 is 128 plus SIGKILL's 9.
Draining deletes the pod; it does not restart a container in place.

prompt: Why does Kubernetes throttle a container at its CPU limit but kill one at its memory limit?
hint: Which of the two can be handed back a moment later?

choices.text: Memory is more expensive than CPU time
choices.why: Price plays no part in how a limit is enforced.

choices.text: CPU limits are only a suggestion to the kernel
choices.why: `capped` ran ten times slower; the limit was enforced.

choices.text: Only a dead process gives memory back
choices.why: Right. CPU time can wait; the kernel can pause a process, but not take back what it allocated.

choices.text: The kubelet chooses between the two at random
choices.why: Both are enforced the same way every time.

prompt: `hungry` had memory request and limit both at 64Mi, and its class was `Burstable`. What would make it `Guaranteed`?

choices.text: A CPU request and limit, equal
choices.why: Right. Then every container has both resources with requests equal to limits.
Then request and limit would differ, which is still Burstable.
Kubernetes would fill it in from the limit; CPU would still be missing.

choices.text: A `qosClass: Guaranteed` field in the spec
choices.why: The class lives in the status and is derived, never written.

prompt: A pod has no requests and no limits. What is its class?

choices.why: Burstable needs at least one request or limit.
Right. Nothing written, nothing promised.
Guaranteed needs limits on both resources.
`probe` ran without either.
